sections.name: Results
sections.text:
This section comprises three parts: understanding the optimization 
dynamics of Augmented Memory45 using a toy MPO task, benchmark-
ing against 15 models (including dataset-screening baselines) on MPO 
docking tasks and directly optimizing for DFT electronic properties 
as a high-fidelity oracle. Every experiment was run across ten seeds 
(0–9 inclusive) excluding the DFT experiments due to high compu-
tational costs (three seeds, 0–2 inclusive instead). The oracle budget 
(number of unique molecules assessed) is varied across experiments to 
enable a fair comparison with previous works and will be clearly stated.
Part 1: elucidating the optimization dynamics of 
Augmented Memory
We begin by identifying the optimal architecture and hyperparameters 
of Augmented Memory45. First, we experiment with varying the batch 
size and augmentation rounds of the Augmented Memory algorithm 
across the RNN11, decoder transformer16,17 and Mamba49 backbones. 
Next, we illustrate the sample efficiency–diversity trade-off and dem-
onstrate that local exploitation in the chemical space can be a vital 
mechanism for sample efficiency.
Experimental details: we define a toy experiment with the follow-
ing MPO objective: molecular weight of <350 Da; number of rings, ≥2; a 
nd maximize topological polar surface area47. Optimizing this objec-
tive requires generating molecules with rings saturated with heter -
oatoms, which are dissimilar from the training data. Hence, it is also 
testing out-of-support optimization. The oracle budget is 1,000 and 
the models were pretrained with ChEMBL 33 (ref. 50; Supplementary 
Section 1.6).
Metrics: the sample efficiency metrics are yield and oracle bur -
den (OB). Yield is the number of unique generated molecules above 
a reward threshold, and OB is the number of oracle calls required to 
generate N unique molecules above a reward threshold. The reward 
threshold in this experiment is 0.7 as molecules start to possess satu-
rated heteroatom rings. Most configurations generate at least some 
molecules passing this threshold within the budget, enabling us to 
report statistics.
Understanding the limits of Augmented Memory across back -
bones: Augmented Memory 45 is a reinforcement learning (RL) algo -
rithm that improves the sample efficiency by repeated learning 
from high-reward SMILES. We hypothesized that as long as unique 
high-reward SMILES are still generated, sample efficiency can 
improve with decreasing batch size, at the expense of diversity. Here 
repeat-generated SMILES do not impose additional oracle evalua -
tions as we retrieve their rewards from a cache using SMILES canoni-
calization matching. We perform a grid search and vary the batch size 
(64, 32, 16 and 8) and augmentation rounds (0–20) across architec -
ture backbones with similar parameter counts: RNN11 (5.8M), decoder 
transformer16,17 (6.3M) and Mamba49 (5.2M) (Supplementary Section 2 
provides comprehensive results). Extended Data Table 1 contrasts the 
performance across the backbones given this hyperparameter range: 
increasing augmentation rounds improves the sample efficiency met-
rics (yield and OB). However, this trend is more consistent for Mamba 
in which the improvements are generally monotonic. In the most chal-
lenging OB 100 metric, Mamba is successful in 10/10 replicates, com-
pared with only 5/10 and 4/10 for RNN and transformer, respectively 
(Extended Data Table 1). Given Mamba’s improved sample efficiency, 
we focus our analysis on comparing it with the RNN baseline in the 
remainder of this section (decoder transformer results are provided 
in Supplementary Section 2.2).
Sample efficiency–diversity trade-off: we fix the Mamba back -
bone to better understand the interplay between batch size, aug -
mentation rounds, yield and diversity. Figure 2a (left) shows that 
increasing augmentation rounds generally increases yield, but is incon-
sistent at low batch sizes (8). This is expected since the approxima -
tion to the expected reward (equation (3)) becomes more noisy. Yield 
validation1. Subsequently, the most promising candidates from docking 
are subjected to higher-fidelity oracles, particularly molecular dynam-
ics simulations, which can offer a much more accurate estimation of 
binding affinity7. Directly optimizing high-fidelity oracles offers the 
potential to greatly improve the quality of the generated set8. However, 
doing so is impractical due to computational cost, exemplifying the 
sample efficiency problem. Either simulation protocols become much 
faster without sacrificing accuracy, or generative models become suf-
ficiently efficient to optimize under an acceptable oracle budget. We 
note that quantitative structure–activity relationship models are often 
used, which can have great predictive accuracy, but may suffer from a 
narrow domain of applicability (within their training data)9.
Existing works have tackled generative design using a variety 
of architectures, including simplified molecular-input line-entry 
systems (SMILES) 10-based recurrent neural networks (RNNs) 11–15, 
transformers 16 –20, variational autoencoders 21– 24, adversarial 
approaches 25,26, graph-based models 3,26–28, GFlowNets 29, genetic 
algorithms (GAs)5,30, and diffusion or flow-based models 4,31–33. Long 
short-term memory RNNs11 have also been used as a predictive model 
within a GA workflow to generate self-assembling peptides, thereby 
serving as a fitness function34.
Despite the recent trend towards three-dimensional molecular 
generation31–33, language-based models are amongst the most sample 
efficient35–37 and can satisfy three-dimensional-dependent objectives 
such as docking. Accordingly, text is still one of the most widely used 
molecular representations10,38 for generative design, with recent model 
architectures expanding beyond RNNs and transformers to structured 
state space sequence models39. The non-injective syntax of SMILES can 
confer advantageous properties for generative design. Specifically, a 
single molecule can be expressed as at least N (number of heavy atoms) 
SMILES, in a process known as SMILES augmentation, enumeration or 
randomization40. This mechanism can be exploited to pretrain models 
under low-data regimes41–43, improve sample efficiency44,45 and perform 
transfer learning with a single positive example46.
The release of the practical molecular optimization benchmark35 
highlighted that improvements in sample efficiency is practically 
important. Accordingly, more recent studies3–5,45,47 have enforced fixed 
oracle budgets compared with other methods, with language-based 
models still amongst the best performing ones. More recently, Guo 
et al. proposed Augmented Memory, which combines experience 
replay48 with SMILES augmentation40 to improve sample efficiency. In 
this work, we release Saturn as a framework for generative molecular 
design. First, we elucidate the mechanism of Augmented Memory as the 
original work only showed its empirical benefits. Next, we systemati-
cally assess language-based architectures including RNNs11, decoder 
transformers16,17 and the recent Mamba49 model. Our results show that 
Mamba intensifies the effect of data augmentation and experience 
replay to improve sample efficiency by strategic overfitting. Our con-
tributions are as follows:
• We elucidate the mechanism into how data augmentation, expe-
rience replay, and reinforcement learning improves sample 
efficiency.
• We comprehensively evaluate language model backbones includ-
ing RNN, decoder transformer and Mamba, which enables us to 
characterize model-intrinsic and scaling properties that lead to 
improved sample efficiency.
• We propose a molecular generation framework called Saturn 
(Fig. 1), and show that the use of the Mamba architecture with the 
Augmented Memory 45 optimization algorithm outperforms 15 
models on multiparameter optimization (MPO) drug discovery 
tasks under heavily constrained oracle budgets.
• Using the same setup, we demonstrate the direct optimization 
of electronic properties with full geometry optimization at the 
density functional theory (DFT) fidelity level.

improvements are more notable at lower batch sizes (16 and 8) with 
increasing augmentation rounds but comes at the expense of diversity 
(Fig. 2a (middle)). In this plot, batch size 8 with high augmentation 
rounds leads to high variance and a sharper diversity trade-off. Focus-
ing on batch size 16, Fig. 2a (right) illustrates the efficiency–diversity 
Pareto front. The default hyperparameters in this work (batch size 
16 and 10 augmentation rounds) balance sample efficiency and diver-
sity and bounding variance. Taken together, these results corroborate 
the efficiency–diversity trade-off noted in previous works35, but goes 
further to explicitly show how this can be modulated by the batch 
size and augmentation rounds. Next, we posit that adding a GA, that 
is, GraphGA30, as part of the generative process can better maintain 
diversity, but we were interested in its effect on sample efficiency. 
Fixing the batch size to 16 (still using Mamba), we ran another grid 
search varying the augmentation rounds but now also with the GA 
activated: at every generation epoch, the GA was applied to the replay 
buffer, and five or ten resulting molecules were randomly selected 
and added to the sampled batch for RL. Note that since the reward 
function needs to be evaluated for these GA-derived molecules, this 
entails allocating a portion of the oracle budget to the GA. There are 
three main observations from Fig. 2b (left). (1) The results reaffirm that 
increasing the augmentation rounds generally increases yield, at the 
expense of diversity. (2) With the GA activated, the yield improves to 
a lesser degree but diversity is maintained. (3) Allocating more of the 
oracle budget to the GA (Saturn-GA-10) leads to a lower yield. Next, 
focusing on illustrating the effect of the GA on diversity, Fig. 2b (right) 
shows that activating the GA maintains diversity even with increasing 
augmentation rounds.
Considering the results from this section, it is clear that lower 
batch sizes and higher augmentation rounds with SMILES augmen-
tation together with the GA are tools that modulate the efficiency–
diversity trade-off. Practically, this implies that in situations where 
generating as many optimal solutions as possible is important, lower 
batch sizes and higher augmentation rounds can be advantageous. 
Conversely, if solutions should be more diverse, higher batch sizes, 
lower augmentation rounds and GA may be better suited. In the remain-
der of the main experiments, we do not use the GA (Supplementary 
Section 2.4 provides more GA results). Thus far, the results validate the 
efficiency–diversity trade-off, but why does Mamba outperform RNN?
Higher model capacity can benefit sample efficiency: Mamba 
(5.2M) and RNN (5.8M) have similar parameter counts, but during 
pretraining, the former converges to a lower loss (Supplementary Sec-
tion 1.6). Mamba generates repeated SMILES (Extended Data Table 1), 
suggesting it overfits the data distribution. Figure 2c shows that with 
high augmentation rounds, the average maximum conditional token 
probability during generation approaches 1 (less so for RNN). This 
makes it likely—but not deterministic—to generate the same SMILES 
repeatedly. The results suggest that increased capability to model 
distributions can improve the sample efficiency, which naturally raises 
the question: can RNN (and decoder transformer) also achieve this? 
From a modelling perspective, one would expect that increasing the 
parameter count will enhance distribution matching. We verify this 
in Supplementary Section 5.7 and show that larger RNN and decoder 
transformers (>20M) can match the performance of Mamba (5.2M). 
Thus, these results affirm that enhanced distribution matching is not 
unique to Mamba. We use Mamba as the default architecture solely 
because it is more parameter efficient in our experiments. We next set 
out to better understand what exactly Augmented Memory is doing.
Squeezing the likelihood of augmented SMILES: although the 
original Augmented Memory work45 demonstrated its empirical ben-
efits, we elucidate the underlying mechanism. T o isolate its effect, 
we design a subexperiment as follows: generate molecules until the 
buffer is full (100) and then save the agent checkpoints before and 
after executing Augmented Memory (10 augmentation rounds) and 
save every augmented SMILES form (total, 1,000 SMILES). After exe-
cution, the (end) agent becomes more likely to generate the set of 
augmented SMILES (Fig. 2d, top). The more improbable the SMILES

when the logits are tuned (Fig. 2d, bottom). Despite this, there is still 
a clear negative slope observed. Focusing on Fig. 2d (bottom), there 
are cases in which ΔNLL is positive after Augmented Memory, that is, it 
actually becomes less likely to generate the specific SMILES sequence. 
This observation is explained by the loss function (equation (5)), which 
is defined as the squared difference between the Augmented and Agent 
Likelihoods, and can be zero for some values. In this scenario, ΔNLL 
is dictated by the other SMILES in the batch. Conversely, as long as 
these likelihoods remain different, the loss function can push up the 
likelihood of all augmented SMILES. Therefore, Augmented Memory 
squeezes the likelihoods of generating augmented SMILES sequences 
towards the most likely one.
Mamba—hop and locally exploit: in the previous section, we 
showed that the agent becomes increasingly likely to generate the 
buffer molecules, as summarized by the regression line in Fig. 2d. We 
hypothesized that Mamba exhibits a hop and locally exploit behav -
iour. Because it may generate some SMILES representation of these 
molecules (strategic overfitting), small changes to any tokens in these 
augmented sequences equates to small changes to the same molecular 
graph, essentially performing a local exploitation (similar molecules, 
on average, exhibit similar properties). We verify our hypothesis with 
the following experiment: generate 3,000 molecules and separate the 
generated set into ten chunks (300 SMILES each). We trace the gener-
ated trajectory using uniform manifold approximation and projection51 
and plot the chunk centroids, comparing Mamba and the baseline 
(vanilla Augmented Memory) (Fig. 2e). Mamba traverses the chemi -
cal space in an increasingly directional manner and the chunks are 
more locally confined. Further analysis into the intra- and interchunk 
Tanimoto similarity reveals that within chunks (top value), Mamba 
exhibits greater similarity than the baseline, and similarity is always 
lower between chunks (bottom values) (Fig. 2f ). Taking these obser-
vations together, Mamba (batch size 16) with Augmented Memory 
(10 augmentation rounds) improves the sample efficiency via the hop 
and locally exploit behaviour. From here on, this model configuration 
will be referred to as Saturn and hyperparameters are fixed such that 
all performance metrics in the following sections are out of the box.
Part 2: benchmarking the Saturn framework and 
demonstrating enhanced optimization
In this section, we follow Lee et al.5 (goal-aware fragment extraction, 
assembly and modification (GEAM) model) and benchmark the Saturn 
framework on MPO docking tasks.
Experimental details: for an exact comparison with GEAM 5, we 
extracted their oracle code for our experiments and pretrained on the 
provided ZINC 250k (ref. 52) dataset (Supplementary Section 5.1). We 
note that the other model baselines were adapted from ref. 5 and these 
model checkpoints were also trained on the same ZINC 250k dataset. 
All models were tasked to optimize GEAM’s MPO objective function 
(equation (1)) for an exact comparison:
R(x)= ˆDS(x)×QED(x)× ˆSA(x)∈[ 0,1], (1)
where ˆDS is the normalized QuickVina 2 (ref. 53) docking score and ˆSA 
is the normalized synthetic accessibility score54 (Supplementary Sec-
tion 5.3 provides the normalization details). Following GEAM5, docking 
was performed against five targets: parp1, fa7, 5ht1b, braf and jak2. We 
reproduced GEAM’s results and ran Saturn across ten seeds (0–9 inclu-

requires the labelled ZINC 250k dataset with all docking values already 
precomputed; therefore, there is a large upfront oracle cost (250k 
oracle calls, across five targets, equating to 1.25 million docking 
simulations).

hit ratio (%) (with the additional constraint of maximum Tanimoto simi-
larity of 0.4 to the training data). We further propose strict hit ratio (%) 
and strict novel hit ratio (%), which filter for the more stringent criteria 
of QED > 0.7 (based on the DrugStore dataset of marketed drugs55) and 
SA < 3 (based on off-the-shelf catalogue molecules54). Although drug 
candidates need not necessarily meet these stricter thresholds, this 
metric that assesses optimization capability, which becomes pertinent 
when jointly optimizing all components, is especially crucial. From an 
optimization perspective, the objective function (equation (1)) aims 
to maximize QED and minimize SA and docking score simultaneously. 
Therefore, achieving high QED and low SA is part of the goal itself. We 
additionally measure molecular diversity using IntDiv1 (ref. 56) and 
#Circles57 with a distance threshold of 0.75.
The Saturn framework and GEAM outperform all baselines. We 
evaluate the hit ratio and include the random sampling of 3,000 mol-
ecules from ZINC 250k (ref. 52) and ChEMBL 33 (ref. 50) as the baselines 
(Table 1). The results show that only Augmented Memory45, Molecular 
Out-Of-distribution Diffusion (MOOD)4, GEAM5 and Saturn outperform 
these baselines, with GEAM and Saturn displaying similar performance. 
For the novel hit ratio (Extended Data Table 2), GEAM outperforms 
Saturn, which generates molecules more similar to the ZINC 250k 
pretraining dataset. T o demonstrate how to satisfy this ‘novel‘ met-
ric, we divide the task into two phases, akin to curriculum learning58. 
First, we task the base Saturn framework to generate molecules with 
a high Tanimoto dissimilarity (this is, the only optimization objec -
tive) to ZINC 250k (1,500 oracle calls). This new model checkpoint 
(Saturn–Tanimoto) is the new starting point for GEAM’s MPO task. 
Extended Data Table 2 shows that the performance immediately recov-
ers and matches GEAM. We believe this is still a fair assessment as 
computing the Tanimoto similarity is inexpensive (this process took 
minutes) and also shows the flexibility of the framework.
Saturn framework: enhanced MPO. Next, we assess the optimiza-
tion capability of GEAM and the Saturn framework by applying a strict 
filter for QED > 0.7 and SA < 3 (Table 2). The results show that GEAM’s 
hit ratios notably drop, whereas Saturn’s remain relatively unchanged, 
which demonstrates that Saturn optimizes the MPO objective to a 
much greater degree (Supplementary Section 5.5 shows the novel 
strict filter results). Importantly, Saturn finds molecules passing this 
strict filter with much fewer oracle calls (the OB metrics are listed in 
Table 2), trading off diversity to do so. For fa7 and braf, GEAM does not 
find 100 molecules passing the strict filter in 9/10 and 4/10 replicates, 
respectively, whereas Saturn is successful in 10/10 for both (Table 2).
T o further investigate the optimization capability, we pool all mol-
ecules across the ten seeds and plot the reward distributions comparing 
random sampling from the ZINC 250k pretraining dataset, GEAM and 
Saturn (Fig. 3). GEAM molecules have a similar reward distribution to 
random sampling, whereas Saturn notably shifts the reward higher. 
The reason why GEAM and random sampling have similar reward dis-
tributions is because the MPO function (equation (1)) jointly considers 
QED, SA score and docking score. Although GEAM molecules possess 
better docking scores than random sampling, QED and SA score are less 
optimal (Supplementary Fig. 6). Supplementary Table 27 also shows 
that the GEAM-generated molecules have a higher molecular weight 
and lower ligand efficiency (docking score divided by the number of 
heavy atoms) compared with Saturn-generated molecules. Finally, 
Fig. 3 also displays the top-two (by reward) pooled molecules with 
an ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity of <0.4. Here the results illustrate that 
GEAM molecules have more favourable docking scores than random 
sampling, but the QED and SA score are less optimal. By contrast, Saturn 
jointly optimizes all objectives to a greater degree, ultimately explain-
ing why the reward distribution is shifted to higher values.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
In this work, we present Saturn, a framework for sample-efficient 
de novo molecular design. We use the Mamba49 architecture with RL 
and show how it intensifies the effect of Augmented Memory45, which 
combines SMILES augmentation and experience replay for enhanced 
sample efficiency. We elucidate the mechanism of Augmented Memory 
and show it makes generating varying SMILES forms of the replay buffer 
molecules more likely (Fig. 2d). By investigating the sample efficiency–
diversity trade-off across architectures (long short-term memory 11 
RNN, decoder transformer16,17 and Mamba49), we show that models 
with increased distribution learning capacity enhance Augmented 
Memory’s effect. This leads to generated molecules being more similar, 
which can be beneficial for sample-efficient optimization, but comes 
at the expense of sample diversity.
The Saturn framework can directly optimize for high-fidelity ora-
cles, such as DFT, as shown in the ‘Part 3: directly optimizing electronic 
properties at the DFT fidelity level’ section. However, there are two 
particularly important limitations we highlight. First, methods such as 
molecular mechanics Poisson–Boltzmann surface area61 or free energy 
perturbation7 generally have improved predictive accuracy of binding 
affinity over molecular docking used in this work. Accordingly, existing 
studies have generated molecules directly optimizing for molecular 
mechanics Poisson–Boltzmann surface area62 or absolute free energy 
perturbation8. Although the current Saturn framework was validated

binding affinity oracles. Another limitation is the synthesizability 
of the generated molecules. Although some experiments incorpo -
rated the SA score 54 in the optimization objective, running explicit 
retrosynthetic analysis would better assess synthesizability and guide 
the model towards the synthesizable space63. Subsequently, follow-up 
works have coupled retrosynthesis models with the Saturn framework 
to enable generating molecules predicted to be synthesizable using 
specific building block sets, enforcing or avoiding specific reactions 
and minimizing the synthesis route length64,65.
Augmented Memory algorithm 45 makes generating the replay 
buffer molecules more likely, leading to local exploitation. In the case 
studies performed, this behaviour was beneficial for sample efficiency. 
However, this will not generalize to every optimization objective, as 
structure–property relationships can impose troughs in the reward 
signal. A concrete and extreme example is a steep ‘activity cliff’ in which 
a small change (even a single atom) elicits a large property value differ-
ence (for instance, binding affinity)66. In these scenarios, generating 
similar molecules can be disadvantageous and a more exploratory 
strategy would probably perform better. Therefore, an important 
research avenue is to characterize the failure modes of the Saturn 
framework and enable future generative workflows to more optimally 
or adaptively balance the exploration–exploitation trade-off when 
faced with an arbitrary optimization objective. Relatedly, existing stud-
ies have investigated parallel generative models, each separately tasked 
with exploration and exploitation 67, or an ensemble of cooperating 
generative models to better navigate the design space68.

In this section, each component of the Saturn framework (Fig. 1) is 
described: the language model backbone for molecular generation, 
the Augmented Memory45 RL algorithm, the GA, and specific details 
into key components responsible for sample efficiency and mitigat -
ing mode collapse.
Autoregressive language model backbone for molecular genera-
tion: molecules are represented as SMILES 10 and the task of 
goal-directed generation is cast as an RL problem. Let S t denote the 
state space representing all intermediate token sequences during 
molecular generation. The action space, At(st), is defined as the condi-
tional token distribution induced by the policy, πθ, and parameterized 
by a language model backbone. In this work, we investigated RNN, 
decoder transformer and Mamba backbones with the latter chosen as 
the default after extensive experimentation. Therefore, θ represents 
the parameters of the Mamba backbone 49,69, which is a state space 
model70,71 and features four learnable matrices to propagate sequence 
information ̄A, ̄B, ̄Cand ̄D:
ht = ̄Aht−1 + ̄B(xt)xt
yt = ̄C(xt)ht + ̄Dxt,
where h is the state, x is the input sequence (SMILES in this work) and 
y is the output. Importantly, the input-dependent parameters confer 
a selective mechanism that can handle contextual importance, and 
notably differs from previous state space models 70,71. Like other lan-
guage models, a linear projection transforms the Mamba output to 
a multinomial token distribution. This enables sequence generation, 
which we define as a Markov process, and thus, sampling a SMILES, x, is

approximated by sampling a batch, B, of SMILES. The batch size con-

is necessarily more noisy. Supplementary Section 1.5 provides com -
plete details on the algorithm and pseudo-code.
Augmented Memory: in the Saturn framework, Augmented 
Memory maintains a replay buffer of the top-100 SMILES ranked by 
their rewards. At each generation epoch, the agent is updated N aug-
mentation rounds times. Each augmentation round involves taking 
every SMILES in the buffer, augmenting (randomizing) 40 them and 
updating the agent following equation (5 ). A diversity filter 73 stores 
the Bemis–Murcko74 scaffolds of every SMILES generated. If a scaffold 
is generated more than a permitted threshold (M = 10 in this work), its 
reward is truncated to 0. Before executing Augmented Memory, scaf-
folds associated with penalized rewards are purged from the buffer, 
preventing mode collapse.
GA: the Saturn framework adapts GraphGA30 in which the replay 
buffer is treated as the parent population. In this work, the replay buffer 
stores the top-100 SMILES generated so far (by reward) and serves as 
the parent population. When activated, at each generation epoch, 
the GA performs ‘cross-over’ and ‘mutation’ operations. Concretely, 
the two parents are selected from the pool of top-100 SMILES with a 
probability proportional to their reward and converted to RDKit75 ‘Mol’ 
graphs. All GA operations are performed on this molecular graph repre-
sentation. Cross-over selects, with equal probability, cutting the parent 
molecules either at ring or non-ring positions. The resulting frag -
ments are combined to produce the ‘child’ molecule. In particular, the 
child molecule is only kept if it satisfies the following hard constraints: 
15 < number of atoms < 40, the maximum ring size is <7, no allenes in 
rings and no double bond in a three- or four-membered ring. Subse -
quently, the child molecule undergoes random mutation operations 
that can include inserting or deleting atoms, changing atoms or chang-
ing bonds. In total, 100 molecules are produced using the GA and a sam-
pled subset is added to the generative model’s sampled batch before 
executing Augmented Memory. Our main hypothesis is as follows: 
since Augmented Memory learns repeatedly from the same molecules, 
this inherently causes the agent to generate less diverse molecules 
over time. For Augmented Memory to enhance the sample efficiency, 
the replay buffer should be populated by high-reward molecules. 
Therefore, our main hypothesis is that executing GraphGA on these 
high-reward molecules will, on average, yield other molecules that 
are also high reward and more diverse. Since GA-resulting high-reward 
molecules will refresh the buffer, gaining access to diverse, high-reward

molecules might be able to offer a better sample efficiency–diversity 
trade-off. Implementation wise, after executing GraphGA on the replay 
buffer molecules, we experiment with selecting five or ten GA-derived 
molecules to keep by either (1) random sampling or (2) selecting based 
on dissimilarity (Tanimoto Morgan fingerprint) to the buffer molecules. 
Supplementary Section 2.4 provides more details.
